title: Suspect in Idaho restaurant shooting died of self-inflicted gunshot wound, police say
summary: Twin Falls police chief believes Chad Williams, 24, was alone in Saturday attack that killed three people
body: Authorities say the man accused of opening fire at a fast-food restaurant in Idaho is dead from a self-inflicted gunshot wound, as investigators say quick action by an off-duty law enforcement officer and an armed bystander helped prevent even more bloodshed. Speaking on Sunday, Matthew Hicks, the Twin Falls police chief, said investigators are confident 24-year-old Chad Williams carried out Saturday’s attack alone. The shooting left three people dead and seven others injured at the recently opened restaurant in Twin Falls, a southern Idaho city of about 56,000 residents. Officials said on Sunday that two of the wounded have been treated and released from the hospital, three remain in stable condition and two are still in critical condition. According to Hicks, an off-duty state trooper and an armed citizen, whose names have not been released, returned fire, causing the suspect to move away from the restaurant. “We believe their actions helped drive the suspect away from the scene, preventing further casualties,” the chief said. “We want to take a moment and commend the actions of the off-duty officer and the citizen, and their heroic action to stop this incident.” Detectives are continuing to investigate what led to the attack, Hicks said, adding that Williams’ family has been fully cooperating with investigators. The police chief also pushed back on false claims circulating online that incorrectly identified another individual as the gunman, stressing that the person had “no involvement in this incident whatsoever”. Meanwhile, the owner of the fast-food chain confirmed that one of those killed was an employee. “My heart is broken, my chest is heavy, my eyes burn from the tears I’ve shed. We lost one of our beautiful Associates tonight,” Lynsi Snyder, the In-N-Out owner, said in a statement released early on Sunday on social media. “In-N-Out will be mourning with the families and praying for them as they tread through a very painful season.” The FBI is asking anyone with photos or video from Saturday’s shooting to submit the material as investigators continue to piece together what happened. Police responding to the scene located the suspected gunman’s body near the restaurant, Josh Palmer, the Twin Falls public information officer, said on Saturday. Authorities were still notifying relatives of the victims on Saturday night, Palmer said. The violence erupted around 2pm at the newly opened restaurant, located in a busy shopping plaza where hundreds of people were nearby when gunfire broke out. The Twin Falls resident Haley Dodaro, 43, and her mother went to In-N-Out for lunch Saturday afternoon. While waiting in the drive-thru line, they saw people running across the road and workers bolting out of the restaurant. At first, Dodaro thought there might have been a fire, but then a man directing traffic in a reflective vest said there was a shooter. “So that’s when we knew there was a shooting. People were running out crying and screaming. It was very scary,” Dodaro said to the Associated Press.

title: Rupert Lowe urges Nigel Farage to work with Restore Britain
summary: Lowe says the two should put ‘personalities and our past disagreements aside for good of the country’
body: The leader of Restore Britain, Rupert Lowe, has extended an olive branch to Nigel Farage, saying the two should put “personalities and our past disagreements aside for the good of the country”. Lowe told the Reform UK leader that if he was “prepared to work together around serious policies, serious reform and serious government, then so are we”. In a video posted on X, Lowe said: “I truly believe there could be sufficient common ground for our two movements to cooperate collectively, destroy the looming leftwing alliance that will finish off what hope remains for this country. “In my view, failing to even try because of our own personal difficulties is simply not an option. Now is the time to put our differences aside and cooperate for the good of the country that we all love.” The offer comes after Restore Britain placed fourth in the Greater Manchester mayoral byelection, where its candidate, Marlon West, took 8.7% of the vote. Reform’s Sian Astley came second on 21%, behind Labour’s Andy Burnham’s successor, Bev Craig. Lowe was among five Reform MPs who entered parliament for the first time in the 2024 general election, representing the constituency of Great Yarmouth. The leader of Restore Britain was suspended in March 2025, when accusations emerged that he had bullied staff and threatened chair Zia Yusuf, claims Lowe denied. Lowe founded Restore Britain in February with backing from Elon Musk. Lowe asked Farage to put “personalities and our past disagreements aside” and he set five conditions for cooperation: Mass deportation of illegal migrants “including women and children”. Tougher rules on legal migration, a ban on halal and kosher slaughter, the burqa, cousin marriage and sharia courts. A referendum on the death penalty. Welfare cuts to fund “self-sufficiency”. The exclusion of former Tory ministers from any future cabinet. “Mass deportations must become a political inevitability,” he said. “They must all go.” He cited Reform and Restore’s cooperation on Norfolk county council as proof cross-party working can succeed nationally. Farage framed the next election as “an existential fight to save the country” and said Reform would need support beyond its own ranks to win. “I understand Reform UK will need the support of people from other parties, as well as millions who have never voted before,” he wrote in a post on X. “That is the broad coalition I am building.” He added that Reform has “always been open to anyone” who shares its aims on borders, the economy and democracy, but added: “I will never turn my back on my team.” Farage is fighting a byelection after resigning his seat of Clacton. All other mainstream parties have declined to stand a candidate against him, though there are 34 independents on the ballot paper, including novelty candidates such as Count Binface.

title: RFK Jr tells US families to vaccinate children against measles amid outbreak
summary: Health secretary, longtime vaccination skeptic, spent years boosting misinformation about vaccines including MMR
body: Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, on Sunday told American parents that they should get their children vaccinated against measles, as the surge in infections has reached numbers not seen in the past 35 years. Kennedy, a leading vaccination skeptic who has spent years amplifying misinformation about vaccines, including the shot that protects against measles, mumps and rubella (MMR), made his call in the course of a contentious interview with CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday morning. His remark came as the incidence of measles crossed a milestone – the US has now officially recorded 2,371 confirmed infections so far this year, surpassing the total tally in 2025 of 2,289. Taken together, the past two years have seen more measles infections in the US than the rest of the 21st century combined. The last time a greater number of measles cases were recorded in a single year was in 1991. Kennedy’s statement was extracted from him by Dana Bash, CNN’s host, who invited him to use his “bully pulpit” to talk directly to parents as the new school year approached. She urged him to tell families that they should vaccinate for measles “because it is safe and it will help them save their children’s lives”. The health secretary replied: “Parents should get their children vaccinated for measles. A measles vaccine is effective, it stops measles in about 97% of the cases. People should get vaccinated.” Later in the interview he added that people should also get the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, the main protection against the disease that has been a particular target of the anti-vaccination movement. The health secretary’s call for parents to vaccinate their children for measles contrasts starkly with the many years in which Kennedy has been a leading proponent of misinformation questioning the efficacy and safety of vaccinations. Even since he became the country’s top health official, he has depicted a measles vaccination as a personal choice and claimed inaccurately that the power of the inoculation is waning. The call also comes late in the day, given the rate at which measles is spreading in the US. The 37 new measles outbreaks that have already been recorded this year are putting the US in danger of losing the measles elimination status that it has held since 2000. Kennedy continues to shrug off criticism that his work as a prominent vaccine skeptic, both before and after he entered the Trump administration, has exacerbated the problem. Asked whether he took any responsibility for the measles surge, he said: “Absolutely not.” He went on to blame the outbreaks on religious communities who eschew vaccines and on global health conditions. Any hope that Kennedy’s measles statement might indicate a change of heart were dashed in the rest of the CNN interview in which he turned combative. Batting off questions from Bash, the health secretary responded with personal attacks. He accused the CNN host of “saying nonsense”, “repeating like a parrot” and “making assertions you can’t support”. In one especially demeaning remark he said Bash had become “flustered”. “I’m not flustered at all,” she asserted in a calm voice. “I am frustrated because you are the HHS secretary and you are talking about things that lead to vaccine hesitancy in this country.” In a further comment dripping with condescension, Kennedy told Bash “you probably don’t understand this because you’re not a scientist”. The journalist riposted: “But you’re not, either.” The health secretary’s belligerent approach, in which he at times appeared red faced while frequently poking his finger towards Bash, attracted the attention of commentators. The journalist Aaron Rupar described the performance as “RFK Jr’s epic CNN crashout” and said in a post on X that Kennedy’s “yelling” sounded like “a rabid dog barking”. Andy Kim, the Democratic US senator from New Jersey, took from Kennedy’s comments that he and Donald Trump had no plans to prepare for a possible next pandemic. “The only thing they have a plan for is trying to distract you from the fact that they’ve taken away healthcare from millions,” Kim said. Kennedy used the CNN exchange to spread further misinformation about other aspects of public health. He claimed that both respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) that is a major cause of infant mortality and Lyme disease were caused by manipulation of germs in laboratories. The suggestion has been contradicted by decades of scientific evidence that suggest they both have natural roots. RSV was initially identified in the 1950s, two decades before such experimentation, known as “gain-of-function” research, started. During the interview, Kennedy repeated unfounded claims that there was a link between Tylenol use during pregnancy and autism, and poured doubt on the efficacy of vaccines to protect children against Covid-19. Speaking to CNN’s State of the Union later in the show, Ashish Jha, who advised Joe Biden’s White House on its Covid response, said he was heartened to hear Kennedy say that “every kid in America should be getting the MMR vaccine”. But he added that much else of what the health secretary had said “just isn’t true”. Jha said that the dramatic rise in measles cases on Kennedy’s watch was not coincidental. “The administration has not done enough to promote vaccines. It has not done enough to highlight the harms that come from measles.”

title: Republican calls for Max Miller to resign from Congress amid abuse allegations
summary: Senator Bernie Moreno says congressman and former son-in-law should step down after ex-wife’s allegations
body: Republican senator Bernie Moreno on Sunday publicly called for Representative Max Miller, his ex son-in-law, to step down from Congress amid allegations of domestic and child abuse. As recently as Friday, the Ohio senator had avoided giving his opinion directly on accusations made by his daughter, Emily Moreno, against the congressman. “If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them. He should not serve in the House of Representatives,” the Ohio senator wrote in a post on X on Sunday. “I believe Max Miller needs to seek professional help to end the clear pattern of abuse he has left in his wake. I believe he should not be free to continue endangering others until he does.” Moreno also said he had hoped the situation would remain private but added that Miller’s “increasingly erratic and dangerous behavior has made that impossible”. The senator’s statement came hours after Miller released a livestream Sunday morning denying allegations of domestic and child abuse and insisting he would remain in the race for re-election. The public appearance came ahead of Wednesday’s deadline to replace him on the ballot. “Just want to be clear: no court, no agency has ever substantiated any allegation of abuse against me. No criminal charge has ever been filed against me,” Miller said on the livestream. “Every single one of these allegations were already investigated, and I cooperated fully every single time because I had nothing to hide and I have nothing to hide now.” The statement follows allegations that Miller poured hot water on Emily Moreno, held a gun to her head and broke their toddler daughter’s collarbone. The accusations have intensified scrutiny of Ohio’s seventh congressional district race, with Democrats viewing the seat as a possible pickup while Republicans have largely remained silent so far. When asked on Friday by NOTUS whether Miller should continue his re-election campaign, Moreno responded, “I don’t know,” according to the outlet. Miller, 37, has denied allegations made by both his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, and former girlfriend Stephanie Grisham, the former White House press secretary, as he continues his re-election campaign. Emily Moreno, a conservative policy adviser, shares a two-year-old daughter with Miller. The former couple has been involved in a custody dispute over their child since 2024. In his Sunday statement, Bernie Moreno said it had been “horrific” to witness the situation unfold in view of the public “all while knowing an innocent two-year-old girl is caught in the middle.” Among the allegations, Emily Moreno testified earlier this year in connection with a defamation lawsuit filed against her by Miller that he “took hot water from a pan he had just cooked eggs in and threw it at me”. She has also accused Miller of holding a gun to her head, according to the New York Times. The couple married in 2022.

title: Healey’s profiteering warning on food and fuel risks row with retailers
summary: Chancellor says the government wants to prevent shoppers being ‘taken for a ride’ at the pump or till
body: The chancellor, John Healey, has said the government is standing by to prevent the public from “being taken for a ride at the pump or the till” as the Iran war continues to hit prices. While he said there had been “no significant evidence of so-called price gouging” during the crisis, he used a weekend column to tell the big retailers that ministers were “watching closely” for any signs of profiteering. Healey faces a difficult economic balancing act as the energy price shock caused by the months-long conflict in the Middle East reignites the cost of living crisis. Last week the Bank of England kept UK interest rates on hold as it warned that a further escalation in the Iran war could drive inflation above 4% next year, adding to financial pressures on households. “The conflict affects our national security, our UK bases, personnel and allies in the Middle East,” Healey wrote in the Sunday Telegraph. “But it also threatens our economic security: impacting the family finances of millions of British people. “And I know that many British businesses have been put under pressure by increasing costs too. Conflict and uncertainty increases inflation, threatens growth and pushes up costs for businesses and governments alike.” The comments about profiteering threaten a new war of words between the government and retailers. Amid ongoing public concern about the cost of living, it emerged earlier this year that Rachel Reeves, then the chancellor, had raised the prospect of a cap on food prices to limit inflation caused by the Middle East conflict. The proposals prompted a backlash from supermarket bosses, with Stuart Machin, the chief executive of Marks & Spencer, calling the plans “completely preposterous”. The British Retail Consortium suggested on Sunday that the new chancellor should instead be looking at the effect of tax increases, including employers’ national insurance and business rates, on inflation. Andrew Opie, of the British Retail Consortium, which represents big retailers including Sainsbury’s, Tesco and Asda, said: “Supermarkets operate in a highly competitive environment, delivering the most affordable food in western Europe. The government’s independent competition regulator, the CMA [Competition and Markets Authority], has repeatedly found that fierce competition between retailers, not government action, has kept food prices as low as possible.”

title: Britain could face food shortages as drought continues, farmers warn
summary: Farmers battle to salvage what they can of their crops as heatwave set to continue
body: Britain could face shortages of certain foods after punishing drought in parts of England, the National Farmers’ Union (NFU) has warned as a heatwave was forecast to continue into next week. The UK’s Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has issued heat health alerts for eight regions of England, with temperatures set to rise above 30C in parts of the country. UKHSA said rising temperatures may increase health risks, particularly for vulnerable groups. Farms across the country were affected by floods over the winter, making planting extremely difficult, and now in many areas they do not have access to water as irrigation is being restricted due to drought. It is the third drought in five years and farming groups say this is the new normal for agriculture in Britain. Wheat farmers say their crop is half its normal height, and England is seeing its earliest ever harvest as farmers battle to salvage what they can of their produce. In some areas it has not rained for over a month, while multiple record-breaking heatwaves have hit the country since early summer, drying out the soil. Tom Bradshaw, the NFU president, said this could lead to food shortages and he had asked the prime minister to take action. He told BBC Radio 4 that farmers should be given tax breaks to build water storage systems on their land to prepare for the years ahead. “Those other countries around the world that we currently rely on to produce our food and vegetables, their climates are changing as well,” he said. “It does feel like there is going be some shortages of [food] products.” Climate breakdown is exacerbating extreme weather conditions such as droughts. This summer the Met Office has reported that England had just 8% of its average rainfall for July and it is likely to be confirmed as the driest July on record. About 23 million people across England and Wales are under a hosepipe ban. The dry weather has fuelled devastating wildfires across the country, most recently in Suffolk. UKHSA has issued amber heat health alerts for the East Midlands, the east of England, the south-east and London regions from 9am on Monday to 9am on Wednesday. The north-west, Yorkshire and the Humber, West Midlands and the south-west regions will be under a yellow alert during the same period. Bradshaw said: “Let’s draw a line in the sand and make sure we prioritise domestic food production to deliver growth across the UK.” Cereals such as wheat and barley have been particularly affected, the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB) said. Its first harvest report of 2026 said the hot weather had resulted in the earliest harvest since records began in 2006, with many farmers across the south and east of England completing harvest two to three weeks ahead of the long-term average. Anthony Hopkins, the AHDB’s director of cereals and oilseeds, said: “Across much of the UK, combines have been rolling earlier than usual this year, with many farmers working through the night to avoid the most extreme daytime temperatures. Cereal yields have generally been below the 10-year average so far, with some farms experiencing significant reductions. Following successive years of difficult weather and rising costs, the financial pressures are becoming increasingly acute for those businesses hardest hit.” Anthony Speight, a senior analyst at the AHDB, said: “At this stage, the emerging picture points to disappointing cereal yields in many areas, but we’ll gain a clearer understanding as harvest continues.” Farming is becoming unprofitable as the government removes the EU-derived subsidies that once kept the industry afloat and the climate crisis causes extreme weather that can wipe out any profits from crops. A recent report found a third of British farmers were making a loss or only breaking even. Gavin Lane, the president of the Country, Land and Business Association, warned that for many farmers this could be their last harvest. He said: “Farmers are telling us this is the worst harvest in years. A sodden winter followed by drought has left wheat at half its usual height and some crops not worth harvesting. “This is the third drought in five years. What was once extraordinary is becoming part of farming in Britain, and government must start planning for it. We know that proper government investment in resilient farming systems, from reservoirs to wildfire prevention, could help farmers cope with these new extremes. “Farmers have shown again and again that they can adapt and deliver solutions, but resilience has limits. If we want them to keep feeding the country, they need proper support. Otherwise, this harvest could be their last.” Polly Ashmore, an acting consultant in public health at the UKHSA, said periods of hot weather could result in serious health outcomes, especially for older adults, and it was therefore important that everyone took sensible precautions while enjoying the sun. “We are urging health and social care services in affected regions to ensure they are prepared, and reminding people to look out for elderly relatives, neighbours and those with underlying health conditions, making sure they are aware of the forecast and following the necessary advice,” she said. “Simple steps such as staying hydrated, avoiding the sun during the hottest part of the day and keeping your home cool are some of the key ways to help keep yourself and others safe during periods of hot weather.”

title: Traffic, mobiles, music … let’s turn the volume down
summary: Letters: Readers respond to an editorial on the health impact of noise pollution
body: Your editorial is right that noise pollution deserves to be treated as a public-health issue rather than a mere irritation (The Guardian view on noise pollution: keep it down, 28 July). Yet one obvious source of urban noise receives little attention: modified cars and motorbikes whose exhausts and engines have been made far louder than manufacturers intended. Anyone living in a city or town knows the difference between the background hum of traffic and the explosive revving, popping and roaring produced by a small minority of drivers and riders. These vehicles can wake entire terraces, disrupt outdoor spaces and make life less pleasant for everyone else. What is most baffling is the lack of enforcement. Excessively noisy exhausts are already unlawful, yet action by the police appears rare. Why are police not being held more accountable for enforcing existing noise laws? The MOT regime also seems inadequate. A vehicle can be failed for being “excessively noisy”, but there is no routine objective decibel measurement comparable to the precise testing applied to emissions, brakes or lights. The UK has trialled roadside noise cameras that combine microphones with number-plate recognition, and similar systems operate in other countries. Rolling out such technology more widely would be a straightforward, visible and popular way to improve quality of life in towns and cities. Mark Ebden Frome, Somerset • As someone who is autistic and suffers from misophonia, or extreme sensitivity to noise, I feel noise pollution has increased exponentially since the Covid pandemic. To the problem of leaf blowers and automatic hand dryers (which are so loud I can’t use public toilets that have them), I would add things like public phone use and announcements in public places. For me the problem is so severe that I now struggle to navigate public spaces, but as you point out, such noise pollution affects all of us, even if we aren’t aware of it, with considerable knock-on effects for wildlife. Deana Heath Liverpool • Your editorial struck a chord, although it’s not traffic or nightlife that upsets me, but unasked-for music. I’m a musician and composer, and the way my brain is wired does not allow for what other people call “background music”. For me, it’s all in the foreground. I used to like going to one-day international cricket matches, but they have introduced musical “stingers” to accompany highlights such as hitting a six or taking a wicket. This has resulted in my deciding to no longer attend. It’s the same in restaurants – often waiters cannot turn down the piped racket because it’s controlled elsewhere. Edward Collier Cheltenham, Gloucestershire • Loud music in shops causes me considerable annoyance. After a recent move to Wales, I have been disappointed to find in this “land of song” that a visit even to an upmarket food store involves an aural assault by what can best be described as nasal wailing. Sue Zlosnik Holt, Wrexham • Shrubs, trees and hedges are some of the best sound barriers, as well as good wind breakers and air filters. They are also temperature moderators and good for our mental health. They should be considered essential in urban environments. Chloë Thompson Eynsham, Oxfordshire • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: India’s gen Z have discovered the power of collective action
summary: Letters: The recent Cockroach Janta party protests had widespread support, says Bhaskar Mani. Plus a letter from Nand Lal Rathore
body: A crucial point that your editorial on India’s gen Z protests (28 July) missed out was that the protests the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) launched in Delhi, hunger strikes and all, were not just supported by young, restless or unemployed people. It was wholeheartedly supported by their parents and grandparents, the old and the middle-aged, even well-off young adults with good jobs and little children. And this was not just in Delhi, but across the country in the huge metropolises of Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and Bengaluru, as well as smaller towns. And it was all peaceful, for which credit goes to the ethos of the protests and the CJP. All of this was suppressed in the mainstream media, print and TV, and even distorted to suggest that it was violent in parts. This reflects not just the overwhelming angst and fear of young graduates facing poor prospects, but the significant grievances of a people who are seeing and experiencing their democracy fading away. Bhaskar Mani Bengaluru, India • Your editorial captures an important truth: movements that begin with a single grievance often evolve into broader demands for justice, accountability and democratic reform. India’s gen Z protests are not simply about leaked exam papers; they reflect a generation’s frustration with institutions that have failed to protect merit and opportunity. I could not help thinking about Pakistan. Here, too, students, jobseekers and marginalised communities have long expressed concerns about governance and access to justice. Yet these struggles rarely transform into sustained, nationwide civic movements. Local protests often remain isolated and receive limited attention or fail to generate the solidarity required for lasting institutional reform. Whether in India or Pakistan, young people deserve institutions they can trust, exams they can believe in and public systems that reward merit rather than connections. The significance of India’s movement lies not only in political consequences but in the emergence of a generation that has discovered the power of peaceful collective action. Its long-term impact will depend on whether that energy strengthens democratic institutions rather than deepening divisions. Nand Lal Rathore Chachro, Sindh province, Pakistan • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Solar powers record share of Britain’s electricity mix in July
summary: Farms and rooftop panels contribute 14.4% to the grid – and figures reveal a surge in new installations
body: Solar energy supplied more power to Great Britain’s grid in July than in any previous month as households turned to rooftop panels to cut their energy bills. Solar farms and rooftop panels provided 14.4% of the country’s electricity after some parts of the UK recorded almost twice the average sunshine hours for the time of year. The long spells of cloudless weather helped solar to smash the previous monthly record of 12.4%, set in May. The July reading is 50% higher than a year ago, when only 9.6% of generation was from solar, according to data from the National Energy System Operator (Neso). The surge comes after official figures for Great Britain recorded more new solar power installations in the first half of this year than in any six-month period since 2011. The data, which includes large, ground-mounted solar farms and rooftop panels, tracked 142,536 solar installations, putting 2026 on track to top last year’s record solar additions. However, the lion’s share of the new solar installations recorded are on household rooftops, with these smaller solar systems making up slightly less than a third of the country’s total solar power capacity. More households have fitted solar panels to their rooftops in recent years, hoping to cut their energy bills by generating their own low-cost electricity as fossil fuels have caused bills to rocket, according to energy companies. Chris Hewett, the chief executive of Solar Energy UK – a trade association – said: “Fifteen years ago, solar energy was a footnote in the electricity mix. Now it is a major player, delivering homegrown, cheap, clean and reliable energy.” The extra solar power helped to meet higher-than-usual demand for electricity to run air-conditioning units and fans, providing a rare positive effect of the heatwaves that have led to drought, wildfires and record heat-related deaths across Europe. A typical UK home with rooftop solar powered the equivalent of over five hours of air-conditioning each day during the June heatwave, when record temperatures reached a peak for the summer so far, according to Ember, a clean power thinktank. “The UK is firmly in its second solar boom, joining the trend we’re seeing worldwide, as households and governments look to it as a low-cost and local alternative to oil and gas,” said Frankie Mayo, a senior analyst at Ember. Great Britain’s new solar additions include the largest operating project in the UK at Cleve Hill in Kent last summer. The 373 megawatt (MW) Cleve Hill project dwarfs the UK’s first solar farm, the 1.4MW Wheal Jane solar farm in Cornwall, but will soon be overtaken by the largest planned solar farm in development: the 800MW Springwell solar farm in Lincolnshire, which is expected to begin generating in 2029. Michael Shanks, the energy minister, said: “The lesson is clear: the more power we generate here in Britain, the less exposed families and businesses are to global energy price shocks. That’s how we deliver energy security, get bills down for good and deliver skilled jobs in every part of the country. “Alongside expanding clean, homegrown power, we’re cutting VAT on energy bills, giving families more breathing space this winter.”

title: Karl’s ‘great net zero debate’ was anything but – so beware Coalition claims of renewables taking over ‘two Tasmanias’
summary: One expert described Nationals leader Matt Canavan’s claim of land used for clean energy as ‘plain wrong and plain silly’
body: It was all incredibly matey as Angus Taylor and Matt Canavan strode into cattle saleyards near Rockhampton to meet Karl Stefanovic for a “great net zero debate”. Perhaps a month was long enough for the pair to have forgotten Stefanovic’s left arm being draped around British far-right figure Tommy Robinson and the fawning interview he had given to the anti-Islam activist (an interview that ultimately saw him part company with longtime employer, Nine). But there they were, the Coalition’s two leaders, on another episode of the former morning television darling’s eponymous podcast and YouTube show. “Good on you, Karl,” said Canavan, in front of the assembled crowd. “Wonderful to be here with you,” said Taylor. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Then the “debate” began. Strictly speaking, a debate is where you have opposing views that can thrash out an issue in front of an audience to inform public discourse. But this was not that. Instead it was an entirely one-sided platform for the Coalition to demonstrate their contempt for large renewable energy projects and to repeat tropes about “net zero” and electricity costs. Two Tasmanias? The Nationals leader told the audience that 12m hectares of land would be needed for “solar, wind and transmission lines”. “That’s two Tasmanias’ worth of this stuff across our nation,” Canavan said. Canavan said this figure had come from the “very smart people” at Net Zero Australia – a research partnership of the University of Melbourne, the University of Queensland, and Princeton University. So what did NZAu actually find? In its most recent reporting, NZAu said 2m ha – not 12m – would be needed for renewable energy and transmission infrastructure (slide 36 in this pdf if you want to follow along at home) to help Australia reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions. But that 2m figure represents the total area of projects, not the smaller area of land actually used for access roads, easements and the solar panels, turbines and transmission towers themselves. This “direct footprint” would be about 500,000ha – 24 times less than Canavan’s “two Tasmanias’”. So where did the 12m figure come from? That number was in an earlier NZAu report. It represented the “total project area” estimated for Australia to completely decarbonise its energy system – and also replace all current exports of coal and gas with the equivalent amount, in energy terms, of clean alternatives. That report did not give a “direct footprint” figure, but said, for example, that wind turbines and access roads generally took up 1% of the total windfarm area. Not mentioned by Canavan was that the same report from which he plucked his “two Tasmanias” also estimated a “new forest area of 5.1 million hectares” would be planted to help sequester CO2. The director of NZAu, Prof Michael Brear, said the project had not yet “looked in detail as to how Australia might locate energy infrastructure such that it compromises all forms of land use less, including farming”. “Our latest report has studied related trade-offs between locating energy infrastructure and biodiversity and suggests there may be significant opportunity for managing such risks. “Evidently, estimating the land used by future energy infrastructure is a complex and important topic that deserves careful investigation and careful discussion.” Prof Andrew Blakers, of the Australian National University, has done his own calculation of the land lost to renewable energy in a zero emissions electricity grid – 120,000ha, or 1,200 sq kilometres. He said Canavan’s claim was “plain wrong and plain silly.” “It’s surprising a senator would throw around wild numbers without doing a simple reality check,” he said. Reliability and cost None of this is to discount concerns over the environmental risk from badly placed projects, or genuinely held concerns in many communities faced with renewables projects who are being asked to differentiate real issues from political fear-mongering. Take the repeated evidence-free claim that renewable energy is to blame for rising electricity prices – a constant assertion from the Coalition. Taylor appeared to be road-testing a new phrase during the show saying renewable energy and net zero was “driving up electricity prices, driving down reliability.” But as experts have said repeatedly, this is not true. Australia’s electricity prices have been pushed up largely because of rising gas and coal prices, linked in large part to Russia’s war in Ukraine. But last week the Australian Energy Market Operator reported the price of wholesale electricity – which makes up about a third of the bill from retailers – in the National Electricity Market had fallen by 47% from a year ago. Why? Aemo said in a report that “increased renewable generation” and “higher grid-scale battery discharge during peak periods” had helped lower market prices. Separately, CSIRO analysis has suggested that even if net zero policies were abandoned, the price of electricity in the future is likely to be higher than it is today. And what about reliability? In a recent report, Aemo said that “reliability risks in the next five years are primarily triggered by the retirement of large power stations.” The director of the energy and climate program at Grattan Institute, Alison Reeve, said there was “no evidence” renewables were making the grid less reliable. The reliability standard in place across the National Electricity Market had been breached only twice, she said, both in 2008. “Power outages overwhelmingly are due to network outages when poles and wires are out – a rat gets in a substation or someone drives into a pole. Between 2009 and 2019 only 0.3% of outages were due to a lack of electricity to meet demand.” Plant food? Joining Taylor and Canavan on the panel was the Liberal National MP for Flynn, Colin Boyce. Boyce has previously signed a declaration that dismisses carbon dioxide as “plant food” and that more of it in the atmosphere “is favourable for nature, greening our planet”. Climate change did not rate a mention in the hour-long show, which is a shame, if only because this could have been a chance to ask Boyce if he still thinks that blackouts should be allowed to occur in cities to turn the public away from renewable energy. Graham Readfearn is an environment and climate correspondent at Guardian Australia

title: ‘Stench of sleaze’: Farage struck deal over political return months before 2024 election, reports say
summary: Labour chair accuses Reform of making ‘grubby pacts’ after contradictory reports emerge on timeline of events
body: Reform UK is operating under a “stench of sleaze”, Labour has said, after reports that Nigel Farage struck a secret deal to return as leader of Reform months before the general election. Farage was in discussions about a return to the political frontline from as early as March 2024, despite later claiming he had no intention of returning to politics until June 2024, the Sunday Times reported. In April this year, the Guardian revealed Farage did not disclose a £5m personal gift from the Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne that he received in April 2024. He told senior figures in Reform UK he would need “a million a year” to cover lost earnings if he stood for parliament in the 2024 general election, sources told the Guardian. Under parliamentary rules, newly elected MPs must register any relevant financial interests and gifts received in the 12 months before their election. Farage has repeatedly said he was an “influencer” and media personality at the time of the gift, and was therefore under no obligation to declare the sum. The parliamentary standards watchdog opened a formal investigation over the £5m gift in May. Farage is also now subject to another inquiry over allegations that he was financially supported by the crypto gambler and convicted fraudster George Cottrell, who is a close friend. Farage – who is contesting a byelection in Clacton in a little over two weeks, after resigning over the issue – has accused those raising questions about his financial backing of “demonising” him as part of a “coordinated pile-on” to stop Reform UK. The main parties have declined to field candidates against Farage; his main opponent is now Count Binface, a parody candidate. If Farage wins in Clacton but parliament imposes sanctions for failing to declare the gifts, he may be removed from the House of Commons and face a second byelection. According to the Sunday Times, Farage renegotiated a deal – supervised by Cottrell – to return as the leader of Reform with the party’s then leader, Richard Tice, in March and April 2024. Under the terms of the deal, once Farage became leader, Reform would repay or write off more than £1m in outstanding loans it had received from Tice’s company, the Times reported. The deal was reportedly to have been presented by Farage and Cottrell to the party’s treasurer in mid-May, undermining the Reform leader’s claim that he had no intention until June 2024 of returning to politics. Reform sources told the Guardian that Farage had learned of the party’s liabilities and what loans would have to be repaid if he returned as leader, and any plan had been drafted for if, not when, he became leader. They said he decided not to return, before reversing that decision. Bridget Phillipson, the chair of the Labour party, said that if the revelations were accurate it “blows Nigel Farage’s story apart”. “It would mean Farage was privately negotiating his return to frontline politics while publicly presenting as someone who hadn’t decided whether to return,” said Phillipson. “That raises even more questions about the secret £5m gift from crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne, further undermining his account of why he kept it secret. “Grubby pacts, secret gifts, support from a convicted fraudster, attempted cover-ups and police investigations – it all adds up to a stench of sleaze the public can smell from miles away.” Farage is facing a number of questions about his financial backing aside from the £5m gift from Harborne, which his lawyers said was unconditional and made without the expectation of Farage returning to politics. Financial industry sources have revealed to the Guardian that transactions involving Reform’s leadership have been referred to the National Crime Agency. Farage’s friend and aide Cottrell – known as “posh George” – and his mother, Fiona Cottrell, have been interviewed under criminal caution by Scotland Yard detectives. Sources said that Cottrell, who was jailed for eight months in the US for wire fraud in 2017 and is now based in Montenegro, transferred a total of more than $2m (£1.5m) to his mother in 2024, with each sum arriving shortly before she made substantial donations to the party. Election law stipulates that donations to political parties can only be made by permissible donors including registered UK voters, UK-registered companies and UK trade unions. It bans concealing or disguising donations derived from an “impermissible” donor or the use of “false” information about a donation including the amount or the identity of the donor. Tice has said Fiona Cottrell was a permissible donor and he understood her son was too.

title: The pro-Israel lobby has swayed US presidents since Truman. It must end with Trump
summary: Our new book tracks the growth over nearly eight decades, of the most powerful foreign policy lobby in US history
body: In 1948, with war raging in Palestine, Harry Truman found himself trapped. On one side were Zionist lobbyists and the president’s domestic political advisers, who were urging him to support the establishment of a Jewish state in as much of Palestine as possible. On the other were his top foreign policy and national security officials, led by the secretary of state, George C Marshall. Their unanimous recommendation was to prevent the establishment of a Jewish state, which they believed would trigger war in the Middle East and endanger the future of US relations with the Arab and Muslim world. With the exception perhaps of George Washington, no diplomatic or military leader in American history had a reputation for patriotic virtue and skilled devotion to duty comparable to that of Marshall. Truman was in awe of the secretary of state, who, as chief of staff of the US armed forces, had been hailed by Winston Churchill as “the true organizer of victory” in the second world war. After the war, it had been Marshall who launched the plan named after him to rebuild Europe. In the mid-1940s, Marshall pushed quietly but steadily against the Zionist movement’s proposals to establish a Jewish state in Palestine. He was concerned that American support would open opportunities for the Soviet Union to exploit Arab anger, put Middle Eastern oil supplies at risk in the event of a war between the Soviet Union and the United States, and require the deployment of unavailable American troops to prevent bloodshed and instability in Palestine. These were, indeed, the strongly held views of virtually all of Truman’s most important military and foreign policy advisers. Truman was personally and deeply moved by the suffering of Jewish survivors of the Nazi “Final Solution”, but also irritated by and at times furious with the constant hectoring to which he was subjected by campaigners for recognition of a Jewish state in Palestine, including the World Zionist Organization and a host of other Jewish delegations, friends and politicians. Despite his personal exasperation, he could not ignore them. Coming in an election year that would pit him against Governor Thomas Dewey of New York, pressures from the Zionist lobby forced him into an excruciating and embarrassing position. With Palestine engulfed by civil war, Arab states threatening to invade and the last British soldiers about to leave the country, Truman called a meeting of his top advisers on 12 May 1948. According to Marshall’s own account of the meeting, he warned Truman against adopting the policy strongly advanced by Clark Clifford, his main political adviser, to recognize the state of Israel before it was established. Such a move, according to Marshall, would be a “transparent dodge to win a few votes”, he said, leaving the “great dignity of the office of the President … seriously diminished”. Marshall declared he would not personally be able to vote for Truman should he bow to political pressure on the issue. A shaken Truman closed the meeting by saying he agreed with Marshall. However, within two days, exquisitely sensitive to the tenuousness of his hold on the presidency and the power of Zionist sympathizers to throw New York’s electoral votes to the Republicans, he ordered that the US recognize Israel. *** Today, the influence of the groups loosely known as the Israel lobby has only become more powerful. Truman’s bind – caught between his sense of the national interest and the domestic political price of defying a powerful lobby – was something that, in the decades to come, president after president would experience. To fast forward: Donald Trump’s decision to go to war on Iran earlier this year came after a sustained campaign by Israel to convince the US to join the disastrous operation. It also came in defiance of several of his top advisers, as well as the 45% of Republicans who hold an unfavorable view of Israel. That decision may be most quickly explained as yet another example of the erratic policymaking that define Trump’s two terms as president. But a closer examination of the experience of several of his predecessors reveals that this presidential decision is more the rule than the exception. The fact is that from Truman to Trump, most American presidents have caved to the demands of Israel and its advocates. Driven by the fear of domestic political defeats, presidents have regularly rejected or abandoned foreign policies that both they and their most senior advisers believed were in the best interests of the US and at the expense of making meaningful progress in bringing a peaceful resolution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Our new book, Israel’s Lobby, tracks the growth over decades of the most powerful foreign policy lobby in American history. Comprised of a panoply of organizations, groups and individuals who advocate American policies that explicitly favor the interests of Israel, the lobby was nurtured – and has been encouraged and guided – by Israeli governments. Exploiting the fact that most voters were ignorant or uncaring on the issue, the lobby used enormous resources and concentrated attention to punish or reward politicians at every level depending on their willingness to follow lobby instructions. Over 20 years after the Truman episode, for example, President Gerald Ford launched what he referred to as a “reassessment” of US policy in the Middle East. The initiative had been advanced by Ford and his secretary of state, Henry Kissinger, as a way to escape from two years of embarrassing failures to move toward a comprehensive Arab-Israeli peace agreement. Both Ford and Kissinger had become intensely dissatisfied with Israeli stonewalling. The reassessment was conducted by the committee of “Wise Men” convened by Kissinger: former government officials who had served as pillars of the postwar US foreign policy establishment. The unanimous recommendation of the committee was pressure on Israel to withdraw from the West Bank and Gaza Strip in order to achieve a comprehensive peace, in cooperation with the Soviet Union. Clear indications that Ford intended to accept this recommendation triggered a powerful mobilization by leading Israel lobby organizations, such as the Conference of Presidents of Major Jewish Organizations and the American-Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac). The lobby’s decisive achievement was a letter drafted by Aipac and delivered to Ford demanding that the president “make it clear … that the United States, acting in its own national interests, stands firmly with Israel in the search for peace in future negotiations”, signed by 76 senators. Ford was “mad as hell” at what he believed to be an Israeli campaign to use the lobby to obstruct diplomacy. But he was cowed. To protect his chances for election the following year, Ford rejected the unanimous recommendation from the “Wise Men”, returning instead to the step-by-step process that had so infuriated him, a process of essentially buying slices of the Sinai Peninsula – seized from Egypt in 1967 – from Israel with increasing amounts of aid and then returning them to Egypt. Ford and Kissinger also vastly increased the scale and scope of US support for Israel. That included a sweeping new collection of US political, economic, military and diplomatic commitments made in a US-Israeli Memorandum of Agreement that, along with secret annexes, was signed on 1 September 1975. Aides to Kissinger described the guarantees and concessions made to Israel in these negotiations as “mind-boggling” and “simply incredible”. In his memoir, Ford wrote bitterly about the Aipac letter signed by three-quarters of the Senate that had ruined his diplomatic plans and cast a pall on his election campaign. Indeed, Ford lost the election to Jimmy Carter. The lobby hoped Carter, who won 71% of the Jewish vote, would abandon aspirations for a comprehensive Middle East peace, but he was quick to disappoint. The president set his sights on a peace treaty resolving the core issues of the Arab-Israeli conflict. With high poll numbers and an American public that seemed ready for a commonsense, problem-solving president, Carter voiced his belief in March 1977 in the need for a “Palestinian homeland” as a key feature of the Middle East peace he wished to achieve. The pro-Israel lobby immediately mobilized against Carter’s peace initiative. In a closely held 50-page memorandum for the president in early June, Carter’s senior adviser on domestic political affairs warned him that he would suffer serious consequences, including risks of failing to receive the renomination of his party, as a result of lobby opposition to his public consideration of a Palestinian homeland. Undeterred, Carter offered direct criticism of what he described in an Oval Office meeting as the prime minister Yitzhak Rabin’s increasingly inflexible positions. His differences with Menachem Begin, who became Israel’s prime minister in May 1977, were even sharper. Meanwhile Carter began intensive communications with Egyptian, Syrian and Palestinian leaders. In October 1977, the US secretary of state Cyrus Vance issued a joint communique with Soviet foreign minister Andrei Gromyko committing the superpowers to achieving “as soon as possible a just and lasting settlement of the Arab-Israeli conflict”. Though fully expecting opposition to the president’s Middle East policy, the administration was stunned by the nearly apoplectic reaction to the US-Soviet statement by both the Israeli government and the lobby. Profoundly concerned with the political damage, Carter requested a meeting with the Israeli foreign minister Moshe Dayan in New York. According to Zbigniew Brzezinski, Carter’s national security adviser, who was present at the meeting, “Dayan in effect blackmailed the President by saying that unless he had assurances that we would oppose an independent West Bank and that we would give them economic and military aid, he would have to indicate our unwil…

title: Italy says it’s temporarily suspending EU Schengen arrangement with Spain after 60,000 migrants reach Ceuta – as it happened
summary: The measure will impact people travelling by plane or boat between the two countries
body: Just as we closed the blog, Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni has confirmed the move to suspend the free movement with on air and sea borders with Spain. She said it was “an extraordinary measure, adopted to safeguard national security and prevent possible repercussions for our nation.” In another sign that it may stop short of full border control for all arrivals from Spain (19:19), she said “the measure will be kept in force only for the time necessary, with particular attention to limiting any impact on summer tourist flows.” She added that “Italy is ready to support every European initiative to assist Spanish institutions as needed to restore full control of the Union’s external borders and to address the ongoing situation with determination.” “Defending borders means defending the safety of citizens, combating irregular immigration, and striking at the criminal networks that traffic human beings,” she said. And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today. At least 57 people have died trying to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after as many as 60,000 migrants entered the tiny territory from Morocco (17:33). Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, called it a “a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity” (12:51) and blamed on misleading narratives spread by human traffickers (12:54, 13:17). In response, Italy has moved to suspend its free-travel Schengen arrangements with Spain by sea and air (18:26), claiming it was necessary to safeguard the security of its citizens (19:02, 19:07). It is understood it will amount to “targeted, selective checks” on third-country nationals arriving from Spain (19:19). But by Friday afternoon, the Spanish authorities claimed that a vast majority of the migrants have voluntarily returned to Morocco (16:41, 18:20), with hundreds more going back by the hour as there was no onwards migration route to mainland Spain or the EU (14:02, 15:04). The huge influx, which took place over the course of just 24 hours, overwhelmed the city of 85,000 people, triggered a political crisis for Madrid and led to a barrage of criticism from the US (15:25, 15:29, 18:02) and other EU countries, including broader calls to suspend Spain’s membership of the Schengen area (9:42, 10:21, 12:10, 13:52, 14:52, 16:59, 17:38). If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com. I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa. Spain found an unexpected ally in Slovakia’s Robert Fico, who said that he did not believe that “excluding Spain from the Schengen Area would be the right solution” as he offered help to the government in Madrid. In a lengthy post in English, he said: “I am closely monitoring developments in the migration crisis in the Spanish enclave in Africa on an hourly basis. Today, I also joined the initiative of Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni calling for a strong response from the EU institutions. The Government of the Slovak Republic has long maintained that the most effective way to prevent illegal migration is the rigorous protection of the Schengen external borders. In other words, everything possible – and even what may seem impossible – must be done to prevent illegal migrants from entering the territory of EU Member States without authorisation. It is striking to observe the hypocrisy of many EU Member States, as well as EU representatives, who only a few years ago, through their lax approach, allowed illegal migrants to enter EU countries in massive numbers, causing serious crises. Today, everyone presents themselves as a determined opponent of illegal migration, having seen how voters across individual Member States politically removed several governments because of their inability to deal with the migration crisis. I would like to recall that, several years ago, when I exercised my right of veto and prevented the adoption of mandatory migrant quotas at the European Council, I had to endure considerable political hostility and criticism. Radical, even extreme, proposals will also emerge in connection with the current crisis in Africa. As prime minister of the Slovak Republic, I do not believe that excluding Spain from the Schengen Area would be the right solution. Just as we were prepared to assist France in combating wildfires, Slovakia should also adhere to its proven strategy of protecting the Schengen external borders at all costs. Any country requiring assistance in safeguarding those borders should receive the maximum possible support through the deployment of police officers and the technical equipment necessary for border protection. Slovakia is ready to offer such assistance to Spain.” It looks like not everyone is Italy sees the need to adopt these measures. As Reuters noted, Meloni’s coalition, which came to power in 2022 promising to reduce illegal immigration, has faced strong pressure from a new far-right party led by former army general Roberto Vannacci, whose anti-migrant rhetoric has resonated with some voters. “The problem is that this is ⁠a purely demagogic proposal, as usual designed for domestic consumption and to compete with Vannacci, without solving anything at all,” said Piero De Luca, a senior lawmaker with the centre-left Democratic Party. We are getting a bit more detail on what the Italian decision will mean in practice. The Italian interior ministry said border police would carry out “targeted, selective checks” on third-country nationals arriving from Spain to verify that they had the documents needed for travel within the European Union, Reuters reported. Remember that it’s all a bit symbolic – or political – as all people leaving Ceuta still have to go through a Spanish border control anyway, and do not have free access to the EU or the Schengen zone, as per the EU’s rules (14:02), As mentioned earlier, the issue of migration has become heavily toxic in domestic politics of many countries (14:02), so it may or may not be relevant to just mention in passing that Italy is expected to go to the polls at some point next year – with some media reports suggesting that it could happen as early as April 2027. Italian foreign minister Antonio Tajani has just confirmed the decision to close Italy’s air and sea borders with Spain. In a post on X, he said the temporary suspension of Schengen with Spain “is a necessary choice to safeguard the security of our citizens and defend the European borders.” He stressed that it was “a measure provided for by the treaties and made unavoidable today.” “The migrant crisis in Ceuta reminds us that the management of the Union’s borders is a shared responsibility among our countries, one toward the other. We must work together to prevent uncontrolled migrant flows from entering EU territory, with all the consequent risks and the threat of terrorism, which must be confronted without hesitation.” For what it’s worth, Italy’s reported decision to close borders with Spain follows a specific and direct suggestion they could do just that. As reported this morning (9:42), prime minister Giorgia Meloni said last night that “Italy will not stand by and watch,” and suggested it was “prepared to intervene with extraordinary measures to defend the borders and the safety of citizens, including the suspension of the Schengen Area with Spain.” In the absence of a detailed breakdown of the proposed measures from the Italian government, I managed to get a bit more from the European Commission on what are the legal options available to Rome. A commission spokesperson crucially insisted that “there are today no onward movements from Cueta,” with the focus on “getting the situation under control and making sure people are returning to Morocco.” But they added that: “For the general legal framework, the rules provide that Member States may exceptionally and temporarily reintroduce internal border control as a matter of last resort, to address serious threats to public order or national security (Article 25(1)(c)) Where such threat is unforeseeable and requires immediate action, the Member State may, on an exceptional basis, immediately reintroduce border control at internal borders. The Member State in question would need to notify the Commission, Council, Parliament and other Member States thereof and explain how the situation in Ceuta constitutes a serious threat to their public policy or internal security. As regards maritime travel: What is possible is a reintroduction of internal border control at the internal sea borders. However Article 41 of the Schengen Borders Code provides that the special rules applicable to Ceuta and Melilla remain in place, meaning there is border control between Ceuta and Melilla and the rest of the Schengen area.” The Guardian understands that Italy has not yet formally notified any of the partners of its decision, which may explain why we don’t know the details of the proposed measures yet. There are some precedents: for example, Germany has reinstated some border controls with its neighbours in 2024 as a measure against irregular migration. The latest set of measures is due to expire in September, but German ministers suggested today it would be extended once again. Just like Reuters (18:26), the Italian news agency Ansa says the Italian ministry of interior “has ordered the closure of the sea and air borders with Spain.” It adds that “the decision was made following the most recent information were analysed by the Committee on Immigration and Border Security,” chaired by the interior minister, Matteo Piantedosi. But there are no further details available at this stage. Meanwhile, ever a diplomat, France’s Emmanuel Macron said he had been in touch with the Spanish government to express his solidarity and offer assistance to Spain. “I welcome the ongoing cooperation with Morocco, which has already enabled more than 40,000 returns from Ceuta to Morocco today. The interior ministers are in contact to ensure close monitoring of the situatio…

title: ‘He’s a narcissist’: could Idaho killer Bryan Kohberger win a new trial?
summary: Convicted killer seeks to withdraw guilty plea and go to trial – but that could put death penalty sentence back in play
body: Could Bryan Kohberger, convicted 13 months ago of the murders of four University of Idaho students, now find himself on death row? That’s one potential outcome of a perplexing petition he filed last week in which he claimed he was misled by his defense attorneys into pleading guilty. A new trial could grant the wishes of family members who hoped to see the 31-year doctoral criminology student convicted by a jury in open court and sentenced to death. Or is Kohberger simply following the example of many mass murderers in attempting to gain control of the narrative and extend the suffering of his victims’ families? “I want to make sure that your plea is given voluntarily,” Ada county district judge Steven Hippler had told Kohberger in court last summer. “I want to make sure that you actually committed the crimes to which you’re pleading guilty, because I don’t want you to plead guilty to a crime you didn’t commit.” “Are you pleading guilty because you are guilty?” Hippler asked Kohberger at the hearing before twice reading the specific murder charge tied to each of the four victims. “Yes,” Kohberger responded. Yet in a ruling on Wednesday, Hippler granted Kohberger’s request for a new court-appointed counsel, days after he filed a handwritten petition seeking to withdraw the guilty plea he had entered in exchange for prosecutors dropping the death penalty. He now alleges that his attorneys misrepresented death row by fabricating a story about their “horrific experience” touring that portion of the state’s maximum security prison and claimed he was “advised to lie” and told he would gain a “legal victory” by entering a “false plea”. Kohberger further claimed that his attorneys had failed to disclose what he said was “exculpatory discovery”, including in a recent book Broken Plea that claimed there were chain-of-custody issues relating to the sheath of the 7in knife Kohberger used to kill his victims and was left at the crime scene. He wrote that he “was convinced that actual guilt was not an important factor” in accepting his plea deal, as he could have faced the death penalty. Kohberger, who is serving four consecutive life terms in segregation at Idaho’s maximum security prison south of Boise, told the New York Times he was breaking his silence because “a lot went wrong in those plea discussions. I really do want that to be heard.” The legal avenue open to Kohberger is not an appeal against his conviction for the murders of Ethan Chapin, Kaylee Goncalves, Xana Kernodle, and Madison Mogen in November 2022 – he waived that right as part of his plea deal – but a civil petition for post-conviction relief that could result in a new trial. His move has stunned and horrified the families of his victims. Shanon Gray, an attorney for the family of Goncalves, said Kohberger had become “the mosquito you just can’t seem to swat”. In a statement, he accused the New York Times of giving Kohberger a platform. “People are forgetting about him,” Gray added to the Guardian. “He has this opportunity to file this petition with a deadline coming up so it’s not really a big surprise to us. He’s a narcissist who thinks he’s the smartest.” The Idaho Statesman estimates that Kohberger’s case has cost Idaho taxpayers more than $8m, of which $5.5m covered the expense of the public defense he now rejects. The petition, if it goes forward, could cost a further $2m. Gray acknowledged that the families would have preferred a death penalty trial where the evidence against Kohberger would have been laid out in court. Instead, he said the defendant “received exactly what he asked for: a deal that spared his life. Know this – he hates that life. He wants another chance to roll the dice.” The extent to which Kohberger may simply be seeking attention should not be underestimated, says Rachel Toles, a clinical and forensic psychologist who specializes in extreme violence and serial homicide. “Attention is currency,” Toles said. From a psychological perspective, Toles suggests, Kohberger may be stuck in the same “obsessive loop that he could outsmart everyone by committing the perfect crime. Now that he’s in jail, he’s probably telling himself he can outsmart people with a new trial and win.” Issues of ego, power and control are what often defines mass murderers – even after they have been caught and prosecuted. By seeking a new trial, says Toles, Kohberger is trying to assert control. “He’s no longer letting the prosecution define the ending, he’s no longer letting his attorneys define strategy, and filing a motion restores his agency. In jail you have a lot of time to ruminate. He’s bored and wants to reclaim the narrative. He wants the outcome on his own terms,” she said. “Getting attention and energy from the media and the victims’ families feeds him,” she added. “Even though this may be torturing the families it may also be giving them hope that if the guilty plea is off the table, the death penalty is back on. “He’s dangling a carrot in front of the families because he knows how desperately some of them wanted him to be put to death and they didn’t get what they wanted.” Kristi Goncalves told Newsweek she was confident that Kohberger’s petition would go “nowhere … but in the case that a judge were to accept it and give him a new trial, we’re all for it. So either way, we’re like, it is what it is.” Idaho law asserts that the petitioner “bears the burden of proving that counsel’s representation fell below an objective standard of reasonableness”. That could pit Kohberger against his trial attorneys, who would be called as witnesses to defend against the allegations of incompetence. “It’s going to come down to credibility,” Adam Ondo, a Boise-based defense attorney, told the Idaho Statesman. “Who are you going to believe? The attorney, or the defendant who is accused of rape or murder or forgery.” Idaho attorney general Raúl Labrador said in a statement: “My office stands ready to do whatever is necessary to ensure justice is fully carried out.” Even if Kohberger can prove that leaving his conviction intact would result in a miscarriage of justice and he receives a new trial, the families of his victims may get no closer to understanding why he stole into the house in Moscow and killed four people. In Kohberger’s case, no motive was put forward by prosecutors, and he was not required to offer one as part of his plea. Toles says that may never be forthcoming because there may not have been one. “He does not possess the true introspection to say why he did it. He could give any answer: I wanted to commit the perfect crime or I was pissed off at pretty blondes. He could give any answer and people will say, ‘Ah, that’s it!’” But, she cautioned, that what all mass murderers do. “They will taunt you. Even if they know the answer, they won’t give it away because that’s giving up power and control.”

title: Trump is determined to pursue his trade war – and he may be difficult to stop
summary: The president’s minions have trawled the statutes to restore roadblocks to trade. The invocation of Smoot-Hawley looks especially dangerous
body: Donald Trump may have found the killer weapon to punish countries at will: by imposing tariffs on their exports to the United States. The president has been looking for a new tool since February, when the supreme court struck down tariffs he slapped on virtually all of America’s trading partners based on the International Economic Emergency Powers Act, or IEEPA, on the spurious grounds that the US faced a variety of national emergencies. It’s become a parlor game among policy wonks to predict what new legal justification he would deploy to replace them. Well, it’s probably not what you think. The round-robin tariffs imposed on everybody last Friday, under the argument that America’s trading partners unfairly undercut US companies by importing things made with forced labor, has drawn a lot of attention. The blatantly specious accusation, sitting uneasily alongside America’s own state-sanctioned abuse of forced labor, underscored how low Trump will stoop to get his way on trade. But those tariffs, imposed under section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, do not provide the carte blanche Trump wants. Tariffs under this section are meant to retaliate against specific “acts, policies and practices” that are “unreasonable” and “burden or restrict” US companies. A blanket charge that every foreign country is enabling forced labor and thus hurting American business is unlikely to fly in court. The whole strategy can be challenged as “arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law” or as “unsupported by substantial evidence”. The truly menacing precedent comes from Trump’s decision, made the Monday before the worldwide forced labor tariffs came into play, to foist a 50% tariff on imports from Canada. The White House’s pretext is Canadian discrimination against American dairy, booze and cars, which, paradoxically, came about as retaliation against Trump’s original barrage of tariffs last year. Sly observers, however, have pointed to Trump’s threat to punish Canada for the forest-fire smoke that wafted into the US. Maybe the new duties are meant to soften Canada as talks get under way to renew the USMCA North American trade pact, or to convince Canadians to become America’s 51st state. Or just because “tariff” is a pretty word. The authority Trump invoked to attack Canada is ominous: section 338 of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930, which is the law that choked global trade in the 1930s and helped sink the world into the Great Depression. Section 338 is particularly dangerous because it offers cover for the president to slap trade levies on whatever country he wants under some fairly hazy arguments. Specifically, it grants the president authority to retaliate against countries that do anything to put the United States “at a disadvantage compared with the commerce of any foreign country”. As soon as the president decides this is going on, he is authorized to “declare such new or additional rate or rates of duty as he shall determine will offset such burden or disadvantage”. Until Trump, section 338 was never invoked to impose tariffs. It was mostly used as leverage, to guarantee that other countries treated American products the same as imports from anywhere else. If some country offered preferential access to a neighbor or ally, the US could demand the same terms, or else. This principle is now called “most favored nation treatment,” which is central to multinational trade rules enforced by the World Trade Organization. Trump doesn’t care about such niceties, though. He has a more destructive agenda in mind. And the statute appears to give him semantic wiggle room. He is determined to pursue his trade war. With such a sprawling mandate, he may be difficult to stop. America’s trading partners were elated in February when a 6-3 majority on the court, including two justices appointed by Trump, ruled against his use of the 1977 IEEPA to impose tariffs at will. It was close, though. The court has shown an almost unbelievable deference to the president. It didn’t object to Trump’s spurious invocation of national emergencies – a “public health crisis” due to illegal drugs from Canada, Mexico and China; trade deficits that “led to the hollowing out” of American manufacturing; something something because Brazil jailed its ex-president Jair Bolsonaro for plotting a coup. The justices merely objected to his use of the statute to impose taxes, which are the preserve of Congress. The executive has gotten away with similarly spurious arguments before. In 1975 President Richard Nixon was allowed to invoke the Trading with the Enemy Act of 1917 to slap tariffs on a zipper company from Japan, a country with which the US was not at war. Trump’s lawyers, in fact, argued before the supreme court that this precedent supported the president’s emergency powers to raise tariffs on anybody under IEEPA. Though Trump lost, his menace to the world remains. Since February his minions have trawled through legal statutes across American history to restore roadblocks to trade. Balance of payments crises don’t exist any more. Still, fresh from his supreme court loss, Trump imposed a 10% tariff on everybody by invoking section 122 of the 1974 act, which allows for tariffs to prevent such imbalances. The use of the law is so ridiculous that Trump’s own lawyers, in the IEEPA case, argued before the supreme court justices that section 122 could not be used as a substitute. In 1974, when the dollar’s exchange rate was fixed, a balance of payments crisis could happen when inflows of money from abroad couldn’t cover the trade deficit, forcing the government to sell foreign assets to plug the gap and preserve the exchange rate. These days the dollar floats. If too little money is coming in, it falls, making it cheaper and thus more attractive for foreigners to buy dollar assets, bringing things back into balance. Fortunately, the balance of payments tariffs had a statutory limit of 150 days. But Trump has tried other stuff too. Section 301 has been used many times before, including by Trump against China in his first term to penalize it for its industrial subsidies, which give its producers an unfair leg up. Trump has also relied on section 232 of the 1962 Trade Expansion Act to put levies on steel, aluminum, lumber, semiconductors and autos on specific grounds about protecting national security. None of these authorities, however, grant him the unrestrained blanket power that could be his under section 338. Let’s see what he does with it.
